measurement-001.question: Which value is closest to an optical power of 5 mW expressed in dBm?
choices: About 14 dBm
About 7.0 dBm
About 0.7 dBm
measurement-001.explanation: dBm is a logarithmic unit referenced to 1 mW: P[dBm] = 10 log₁₀(P / 1 mW). For 5 mW, 10 log₁₀5 ≈ 10 × 0.699 ≈ 7.0 dBm. About 14 dBm wrongly applies 20 log₁₀, used for voltage or amplitude ratios, to power. About 0.7 dBm forgets to multiply by 10. For mental arithmetic, 2 times is about 3 dB and 10 times is 10 dB, so 5 mW = 10 mW / 2 → 10 − 3 = 7 dBm. Subtracting one dBm value from another gives a ratio (dB): for example, if light launched at +7 dBm arrives at −13 dBm, the loss is 20 dB.

measurement-002.question: Why must the wavelength setting be set correctly when measuring with a photodiode-based optical power meter?
choices: Because setting the wavelength tunes a filter inside the meter to pass only that wavelength, completely removing stray light at other wavelengths before measuring
Because the photodiode's responsivity (A/W) varies strongly with wavelength, so the factor for converting current to power differs by wavelength
Because a photodiode measures energy rather than photon number, so power is proportional to current at any wavelength and the setting is only for display
measurement-002.explanation: A photodiode sensor measures photocurrent and displays optical power by dividing it by the responsivity R(λ). The responsivity is proportional to wavelength, as R = ηqλ/(hc), and the quantum efficiency also varies with wavelength, so a wrong setting gives a large error in the displayed value. The meter's wavelength setting selects the conversion factor; it is not a filter that rejects other wavelengths. If light at another wavelength is mixed in, it is detected too. Thermal sensors (thermopiles), which measure heat, depend little on wavelength because the absorber's absorptance is nearly constant over a wide range, so they suit high-power measurements, but they are inferior to photodiode sensors in sensitivity and response speed.

measurement-003.question: A diffraction grating with 1200 grooves per mm is illuminated over a width of 50 mm and used in first order. Which value is closest to the smallest wavelength difference it can resolve at 600 nm? (Resolving power λ/Δλ = mN.)
choices: About 0.01 nm
About 0.5 nm
About 0.1 nm
measurement-003.explanation: The number of illuminated grooves is N = 1200 grooves/mm × 50 mm = 60000, so the first-order resolving power is λ/Δλ = mN = 60000. Therefore Δλ = 600 nm / 60000 = 0.01 nm. About 0.5 nm takes the number of grooves as the 1200 in one millimeter, overlooking that the resolving power is set by the number of grooves across the whole illuminated width. About 0.1 nm is an order-of-magnitude error. Using higher diffraction orders raises the resolving power. In real spectrometers, the entrance slit width, detector pixel size and aberrations of the optics almost always make the resolution coarser than this theoretical value.

measurement-004.question: The spectrum of a narrow-linewidth laser with a linewidth of about 100 kHz is measured with a grating-based optical spectrum analyzer (OSA), and the displayed linewidth is about 0.02 nm (about 2.5 GHz). What is the most appropriate explanation?
choices: The laser's linewidth really is 2.5 GHz, and the instrument's value is correct
A spectrum analyzer measures only optical power and cannot show a wavelength width, so the displayed width is just the width of a screen division
The displayed width is set by the instrument's resolution bandwidth; the laser's true linewidth is much narrower and has not been measured
measurement-004.explanation: The resolution of a grating-based optical spectrum analyzer is set by the grating and slits and is typically about 0.01–0.1 nm. When the linewidth of the light being measured is much narrower than this resolution bandwidth, what is displayed is the shape and width of the instrument's own response function. In the 1.55 µm band, 0.02 nm is about 2.5 GHz, more than four orders of magnitude wider than a 100 kHz linewidth, so the laser linewidth has not been measured. Narrow linewidths are measured by heterodyne detection, mixing with another laser and viewing the beat on an electrical spectrum analyzer, or by delayed self-heterodyne detection, which interferes the laser with a copy of itself delayed in a long fiber. An OSA displays the distribution of power over wavelength.

measurement-005.question: An OTDR pulse is launched into a fiber with a group index of 1.468, and a reflection peak is observed 100 µs after launch. Which value is closest to the distance to the reflection point? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
choices: About 10.2 km
About 20.4 km
About 15 km
measurement-005.explanation: An OTDR finds distance from the round-trip time of an optical pulse in the fiber. The speed of light in the fiber is c/n, so the distance is z = ct/(2n) = 3.0×10⁸ × 100×10⁻⁶ / (2 × 1.468) ≈ 1.02×10⁴ m, or about 10.2 km. About 20.4 km forgets the round trip and does not divide by 2. About 15 km ignores the group index and uses the speed of light in vacuum. Real OTDRs have a setting for the group index (IOR), and an incorrect value shifts the displayed distance directly, so it is set to match the cable specification.

measurement-006.question: Which value is closest to the distance resolution of an OTDR (a rough measure of the distance at which two events can be separated, Δz = cτ/(2n)) when using 10 ns pulses? (Group index 1.468, c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
choices: About 2.0 m
About 1.5 m
About 1.0 m
measurement-006.explanation: Light travels cτ/n during the pulse duration τ, but because the time is measured over a round trip, the distance resolution is half that: Δz = cτ/(2n) = 3.0×10⁸ × 10×10⁻⁹ / (2 × 1.468) ≈ 1.0 m. About 2.0 m does not divide by 2 for the round trip, and about 1.5 m ignores the group index. Shorter pulses improve resolution, but they carry less energy, so the backscattered signal is weaker and the measurable distance (dynamic range) is shorter. Short pulses are therefore used for short fibers inside buildings and long pulses for trunk lines tens of kilometers long.

measurement-007.question: Which correctly describes how features appear in an OTDR trace (backscattered light intensity versus distance)?
choices: Fusion splices appear as sharp reflection peaks, and connectors appear as straight lines with no step
Fusion splices appear as gentle steps in the line, and connectors and fiber ends appear as sharp reflection peaks
The trace slopes upward over sections of the fiber that have loss
measurement-007.explanation: An OTDR trace plots the intensity of Rayleigh backscatter from each point of the fiber against distance in dB, giving a straight line that falls with loss (its slope is the one-way loss in dB/km). At a fusion splice there is almost no index discontinuity, so reflection is slight and the line simply steps down by the loss. At connectors and at the ends of cut or broken fibers, the index difference causes Fresnel reflection and a sharp peak appears. Right after a strong reflection, the receiver is saturated for a while and cannot measure; this is called the dead zone. The trace never slopes upward over a lossy section.

measurement-008.question: In a ToF LiDAR that measures the round-trip time of light pulses, which value is closest to the distance resolution when the time measurement resolution is 1 ns? (In air, c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
choices: About 30 cm
About 7.5 cm
About 15 cm
measurement-008.explanation: ToF finds distance from d = ct/2, so for a time resolution Δt the distance resolution is Δd = cΔt/2 = 3.0×10⁸ × 1×10⁻⁹ / 2 = 0.15 m, or about 15 cm. About 30 cm ignores the round trip and uses ct, and about 7.5 cm divides by 4. For an object 150 m away, the round-trip time is 1 µs. In practice, distance can be determined more finely than this resolution with time-correlated single-photon counting (TCSPC), which builds statistics over many pulses, or by fitting the pulse waveform. The maximum range is set by laser power, receiver aperture, target reflectivity and background light.

measurement-009.question: An FMCW LiDAR sweeps its frequency linearly over 1 GHz in 10 µs. Which value is closest to the beat frequency between the transmitted light and the light reflected from a stationary object 100 m away? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
choices: About 33 MHz
About 67 MHz
About 6.7 MHz
measurement-009.explanation: The sweep slope is S = 1 GHz / 10 µs = 1×10¹⁴ Hz/s. The round-trip delay is τ = 2R/c = 2 × 100 / 3.0×10⁸ ≈ 0.667 µs, during which the transmitted frequency changes by S × τ, so the beat frequency is f_b = 1×10¹⁴ × 0.667×10⁻⁶ ≈ 67 MHz. About 33 MHz ignores the round trip and uses the one-way delay, and about 6.7 MHz is an order-of-magnitude error. The distance resolution is set by the sweep bandwidth B: c/(2B) = 15 cm. If the object moves, a Doppler shift is added, so up and down sweeps are combined to separate distance and velocity.

measurement-010.question: Which correctly describes FMCW LiDAR compared with pulsed ToF LiDAR?
choices: Coherent detection makes it resistant to background light and lets it measure line-of-sight velocity directly from the Doppler shift, but it needs a narrow-linewidth laser with a linear frequency sweep
It compares only the intensities of the sent and received light, so laser coherence is not needed at all and an LED gives the same range and velocity performance
Distance is found by directly measuring the round-trip time of a light pulse, so no beat-signal processing is needed, and velocity comes from successive distance differences
measurement-010.explanation: FMCW uses part of the frequency-swept transmitted light as a local oscillator and interferes it with the returning light. Only light whose frequency matches the local oscillator produces a beat signal, so it is resistant to sunlight and light from other LiDARs, and amplification by the local oscillator lets even weak reflections be detected. If the object moves, a Doppler shift is added, giving velocity at each pixel. In return it needs a narrow-linewidth laser whose coherence length exceeds the round-trip path difference, and the technology to sweep the frequency linearly. It is ToF that needs no coherence; in FMCW, analyzing the beat frequency (with an FFT, for example) is the very process that yields distance.

measurement-011.question: What is an advantage of using a wavelength near 1550 nm rather than near 905 nm as a LiDAR light source?
choices: It can be detected directly with silicon photodetectors or SPADs, making the receiver cheaper than at 905 nm and its quantum efficiency much higher as well
The light is almost all absorbed by the cornea and lens and hardly reaches the retina, so high optical power can be used while keeping the eye safe
Absorption by water vapor in the atmosphere is far smaller than at 905 nm, so even in rain or fog the light is attenuated less and distant targets are easier to measure
measurement-011.explanation: Light at wavelengths longer than 1.4 µm is absorbed by water in the front of the eye (the cornea and lens) and is hardly focused onto the retina, so laser safety standards allow much more exposure than at the near-infrared 905 nm. The advantage of 1550 nm is therefore that high power can more easily be used for long range. On the other hand, silicon photodetectors cannot detect 1550 nm because of their cutoff (about 1.1 µm), so more expensive detectors such as InGaAs are needed. Being able to use silicon photodetectors and SPADs is the advantage of 905 nm. Water absorption is larger at 1550 nm, which also makes it more susceptible to rain and fog.

measurement-012.question: Which value is closest to the axial (depth) resolution in air of OCT (optical coherence tomography) using a source with a Gaussian spectrum centered at 1310 nm with a spectral width (FWHM) of 100 nm? (Δz = (2 ln2/π) λ²/Δλ)
choices: About 7.6 µm
About 17 µm
About 3.8 µm
measurement-012.explanation: The axial resolution of OCT is set by the coherence length of the source: Δz = (2 ln2/π) × λ²/Δλ ≈ 0.44 × (1.31 µm)² / 0.1 µm ≈ 7.6 µm. About 17 µm is λ²/Δλ without the factor of 0.44, and about 3.8 µm halves the result once more. Inside biological tissue it is divided by the refractive index (about 1.38), giving a finer value of about 5.5 µm. Wider bandwidth gives better resolution, so ophthalmic OCT uses broadband SLDs or swept sources. The lateral resolution is set by the size of the objective's focused spot and is independent of the axial resolution.

measurement-013.question: In OCT (optical coherence tomography), which correctly pairs the main factors that determine axial resolution and lateral resolution?
choices: Axial resolution is set by the objective's numerical aperture, as in a microscope, and lateral resolution by the source's spectral width (coherence length)
Both are set only by the source's output power
Axial resolution is set by the source's spectral width, lateral resolution by the objective's focused spot (numerical aperture)
measurement-013.explanation: OCT uses low-coherence interferometry: only reflections whose path difference from the reference light is within the coherence length interfere, which isolates depth position. The axial resolution is therefore set by the source's spectral width (wider is finer). The lateral resolution is set by how small the light can be focused at the sample, and a lens with higher numerical aperture gives finer resolution. However, a higher NA makes the depth of focus shallower, a trade-off that prevents viewing a deep range at once. The option with the pairing reversed is wrong. Output power affects sensitivity (signal-to-noise ratio) but does not determine resolution.

measurement-014.question: Laser light at 632.8 nm hits an object moving along the direction of the light at 10 mm/s. Which value is closest to the magnitude of the Doppler shift of the reflected (backward-returning) light? (f_D = 2v/λ)
choices: About 16 kHz
About 63 kHz
About 32 kHz
measurement-014.explanation: When light reflects from a moving object and returns, the Doppler effect acts both on the light arriving at the object and on the light leaving it, so the shift is f_D = 2v/λ = 2 × 10×10⁻³ / 632.8×10⁻⁹ ≈ 3.16×10⁴ Hz, or about 32 kHz. About 16 kHz drops the factor of 2, considering only a one-way Doppler effect. About 63 kHz uses a factor of 4. This is a tiny change compared with the optical frequency (about 474 THz), but interfering the reflected light with the original light lets it be measured directly as a beat signal. This principle is used in laser Doppler velocimeters (LDV), vibrometers and the velocity measurement of FMCW LiDAR.

measurement-015.question: What is the main advantage of detecting a weak optical signal by chopping the light at a fixed frequency and measuring it with a lock-in amplifier?
choices: It extracts only the component at the reference frequency and phase, greatly reducing the effects of background light, 1/f noise and drift
The lock-in amplifier resonantly amplifies the light intensity itself, so more photons reach the detector and shot noise becomes relatively smaller
Chopping the light shifts its wavelength shorter, into the range where the detector is more sensitive, making it easier to detect
measurement-015.explanation: A lock-in amplifier performs synchronous detection: it multiplies the detector output by a reference signal and passes the result through a low-pass filter, extracting only the component whose frequency and phase match the chopper. Its equivalent bandwidth can be made extremely narrow, so most noise at other frequencies is rejected. Choosing a modulation frequency of a few hundred hertz to kilohertz, where 1/f noise is small, also avoids the noise that troubles DC measurements, constant background such as room light, and detector drift. The light intensity and number of photons do not increase. Chopping does not change the wavelength of the light either. This method is widely used in spectroscopy and in measuring tiny absorption in optical components.

measurement-016.question: When measuring the total power of a source that emits over a wide range of angles, such as an LED, why is an integrating sphere used?
choices: The inner wall is a mirror that images the source onto the detector port, bringing light emitted in every direction to a single focus and measuring it directly
Light bounces back and forth inside the sphere and resonates, and the detector sees light built up by interference, raising the sensitivity thousands of times for weak sources
Diffuse reflection at the inner wall scatters light many times and illuminates the wall uniformly, so light proportional to the total power reaches the detector port whatever the emission pattern
measurement-016.explanation: An integrating sphere is a hollow sphere coated inside with a highly diffuse-reflecting material such as barium sulfate or PTFE. Light entering it is diffusely reflected many times, and the irradiance over the inner wall becomes nearly uniform, so the light reaching the detector port is proportional to the total power no matter how the source distributes its emission. With a baffle to keep direct light from the source out of the port, the measurement is independent of the emission pattern. A mirror wall would project the source's pattern onto the detector rather than making it uniform. The light does not resonate and build up; because it spreads over the entire wall, only a small fraction reaches the port, and the sensitivity actually decreases.

measurement-017.question: Two laser beams at different wavelengths, at +3 dBm and 0 dBm, are combined and measured with a single power meter. Which value is closest to the total power displayed? Ignore the loss of the combiner.
choices: About 4.8 dBm
3 dBm
About 1.5 dBm
measurement-017.explanation: dBm is a logarithm referenced to 1 mW, so values cannot be added directly; they must first be converted to mW. +3 dBm is 10^(3/10) ≈ 2.0 mW and 0 dBm is 1.0 mW, and the powers of two beams at different wavelengths, which do not interfere, simply add, giving about 3.0 mW, or 10 log₁₀(3.0) ≈ 4.8 dBm. 3 dBm comes from adding the dBm numbers directly, and about 1.5 dBm from averaging them. Adding in dB is valid only when multiplying ratios such as gains and losses. Combining two beams of equal power gives a total about 3 dB higher than one alone.

measurement-018.question: An indirect time-of-flight (phase-shift) range sensor modulates the light intensity sinusoidally and finds distance from the phase delay of the returning light. At a modulation frequency of 20 MHz, which value is closest to the maximum distance that can be determined unambiguously? Assume the phase repeats every 2π, and use c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s.
choices: About 15 m
About 7.5 m
About 3.75 m
measurement-018.explanation: Light from an object at distance d travels 2d in the round trip, so its phase delay is 2πf(2d)/c. Beyond the distance at which this reaches 2π, d = c/(2f) = 3.0×10⁸ / (2 × 20×10⁶) = 7.5 m, the phase matches that of a nearer distance and the two cannot be told apart. About 15 m ignores the round trip and uses c/f, and about 3.75 m divides by 2 once too often. Raising the modulation frequency improves the distance precision for the same phase resolution but narrows the unambiguous range. Several modulation frequencies are therefore sometimes combined to achieve both precision and range.

measurement-019.question: A time-of-flight LiDAR measures the distance to a diffusely reflecting (Lambertian) wall much larger than its beam. When the distance to the wall is doubled, by roughly what factor does the power returning to the receiver change? Ignore atmospheric attenuation.
choices: About 1/4
About 1/16
About 1/2
measurement-019.explanation: If the whole beam lands on the wall, the power the wall receives does not depend on distance. The wall scatters it diffusely into a hemisphere, so the solid angle subtended by a receiving lens of fixed aperture, seen from the wall, is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, and doubling the distance cuts the return to about 1/4. About 1/16 applies when the target is smaller than the beam, like a point target, so that the fraction of the spreading beam that hits it also falls as the square of the distance (the 1/R⁴ of the radar equation); it does not apply to a wide target like a wall. About 1/2 wrongly assumes inverse proportion to distance. The actual range is set by this falloff, the target's reflectance and the noise from background light.

measurement-020.question: In the knife-edge method, a blade is moved step by step across a laser beam while the total power passing the blade is measured. Which correctly describes how the beam's intensity profile is obtained?
choices: The power itself as a function of blade position is the intensity profile, and the blade position of maximum power marks the beam center
Differentiating the power with respect to blade position gives the intensity profile along that direction (integrated over the other)
The spacing of fringes produced by diffraction at the blade edge is measured and gives the beam diameter, so the power values are not used
measurement-020.explanation: With the blade advanced to position x, the power meter receives the sum of all the intensity on the unblocked side. The measured curve is therefore the integral of the intensity profile (an error function for a Gaussian beam), and differentiating it with respect to x gives the profile in that direction. For a Gaussian beam the radius can also be found from the fact that the blade travel between the 10% and 90% power points is about 1.28w, where w is the 1/e² radius. The power simply changes monotonically as the blade moves, so no maximum marks the beam center. The method does not derive the diameter from diffraction fringes either. It is used for small spots that cameras cannot easily resolve and for infrared or high-power beams.

measurement-021.question: Near a wavelength of 1550 nm, two laser beams are separated in wavelength by 0.40 nm. Which value is closest to their frequency difference? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s; use Δν ≈ cΔλ/λ².)
choices: About 5 GHz
About 500 GHz
About 50 GHz
measurement-021.explanation: Δν ≈ cΔλ/λ² = 3.0×10⁸ × 0.40×10⁻⁹ / (1550×10⁻⁹)² ≈ 5.0×10¹⁰ Hz, about 50 GHz. About 5 GHz and about 500 GHz are off by an order of magnitude from mistakes in converting nm to m or in computing λ². In the 1550 nm band, “0.8 nm ≈ 100 GHz” and “0.1 nm ≈ 12.5 GHz” are commonly used rules of thumb, and WDM channel spacings are also specified in frequency. When the two beams are superimposed on a photodetector, a beat signal at the difference frequency appears, so the frequency difference can be measured precisely with a fast photodetector and an electrical spectrum analyzer. For the same wavelength difference, the frequency difference is inversely proportional to λ², so it is larger at shorter wavelengths.

measurement-022.question: The linewidth of a laser of a few tens of kHz cannot be resolved with a grating-based optical spectrum analyzer. Which correctly describes the principle of the delayed self-heterodyne method used instead?
choices: The laser light is diffracted many times by gratings to increase the dispersion, magnifying the wavelength scale so the spectral width can be read directly
The light is split, one part is delayed in a fiber longer than the coherence time and frequency-shifted, the two are recombined, and the linewidth is found from the beat spectrum width
The laser intensity is measured with a fast photodetector, and the width of the frequency spectrum of its intensity fluctuations is taken directly as the laser linewidth
measurement-022.explanation: In the delayed self-heterodyne method, the laser light is split, one part is delayed in a long fiber, the other is frequency-shifted by a few tens of MHz with an acousto-optic modulator or similar, and the two are recombined on a photodetector. When the delay is much longer than the coherence time, the two beams behave like separate, uncorrelated lasers, and measuring their beat with an electrical spectrum analyzer gives a spectrum twice as wide as the Lorentzian linewidth. The resolution is set by the electrical instrument, so linewidths down to kHz can be measured. However many times light passes through gratings, the resolution is limited to the GHz level, far from kHz. Intensity fluctuations are distinct from phase (frequency) fluctuations, and their width does not give the linewidth.

measurement-023.question: When the noise is white and independent from one measurement to the next, the same measurement is repeated 100 times and averaged. How does the signal-to-noise ratio (amplitude ratio) of the average compare with that of a single measurement?
choices: About 10 times larger; the noise standard deviation falls as 1/√N, where N is the number of averages
It becomes about 100 times larger; the standard deviation of the noise falls in inverse proportion to the number of averages N
It does not change; signal and noise are averaged in the same way, so the ratio stays the same as for one measurement
measurement-023.explanation: Averaging independent noise N times leaves the signal unchanged while the standard deviation of the noise becomes 1/√N, so the amplitude signal-to-noise ratio improves by √N, about 10 times for 100 averages (100 times, or 20 dB, as a power ratio). About 100 times assumes that the noise amplitude falls as 1/N, confusing power and amplitude ratios. The signal adds the same value in each measurement while the noise, with random signs, partly cancels, so the ratio does change. The noise reduction obtained by lengthening the time constant, and so narrowing the bandwidth, in lock-in detection follows the same idea. However, noise that is correlated between measurements, such as drift or 1/f noise, is not reduced at this rate by averaging.

measurement-024.question: Which correctly describes the procedure of the cutback method for precisely measuring the propagation loss (dB/km) of an optical fiber?
choices: Measure the light power just before it enters the fiber, then divide the difference from the output of the long fiber by the length
Launch pulses into one end of a long fiber and find the loss from the slope of the backscattered intensity versus distance
Measure the long fiber's output, cut it near the input end without changing the launch, and divide the difference from the short piece's output by the length
measurement-024.explanation: In the cutback method, the output P₁ of the long fiber is measured first; then, without touching the launch, the fiber is cut a few meters from the input end and the output P₂ of the short piece is measured. The loss is 10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁) divided by the length that was cut off. The input coupling loss and the effect of cladding modes that die out just after the input are common to both measurements and cancel, so the propagation loss alone can be determined precisely. Comparing with the power before the fiber includes the coupling loss. Using backscattered light is the OTDR method, which has the advantage of measuring from one end, but it is not the cutback method. The drawback of the cutback method is that it is destructive, since the fiber is cut.

measurement-025.question: To calibrate the wavelength scale of optical spectrum analyzers and wavemeters in the 1.5 µm band, absorption lines of gases such as acetylene (C₂H₂) are used as references. Which is the reason?
choices: The wavelength of a gas absorption line shifts in proportion to the light intensity, so a reference at any wavelength can be made by setting the intensity in each instrument
The wavelengths of absorption lines, set by vibrational-rotational transitions of the molecule, hardly change with temperature or pressure and are the same in every instrument
Gas absorption lines are several nm wide, so even an instrument whose wavelength is somewhat off can find the absorption without missing it
measurement-025.explanation: The wavelengths of acetylene absorption lines are determined by transitions between vibrational and rotational states of the molecule, so they are intrinsic to the molecule and change only very slightly with temperature or pressure. They can therefore serve as wavelength markers that are the same wherever they are measured, and acetylene, with many absorption lines around 1510–1540 nm, is widely used to calibrate the wavelength scale in the telecom band. The line wavelengths are almost independent of light intensity, so the reference cannot be moved by changing the intensity. The width of an absorption line in a low-pressure gas is narrow, about the Doppler width due to the thermal motion of the molecules (several hundred MHz, on the order of pm), and it is precisely because the lines are narrow that they make precise references. A width of several nm would be useless for precise calibration.

measurement-026.question: A wavemeter moves the mirror of a Michelson interferometer and counts the fringes of a He-Ne laser of known wavelength (632.8 nm) and of an unknown laser at the same time. During the same mirror travel, 100000 He-Ne fringes and 81640 fringes of the unknown laser are counted. Which value is closest to the unknown wavelength? (Ignore the dispersion of air.)
choices: About 517 nm
About 1550 nm
About 775 nm
measurement-026.explanation: Moving the mirror by x gives N = 2x/λ fringes, so for the same travel the fringe count is inversely proportional to wavelength. The unknown wavelength is λ = 632.8 nm × 100000/81640 ≈ 775.1 nm; the smaller count belongs to the longer wavelength. About 517 nm applies the ratio the wrong way round. About 1550 nm comes from finding the mirror travel from the He-Ne fringes as x = Nλ, dropping the round-trip factor 1/2, and then using λ = 2x/N for the unknown light only. Since N = 2x/λ holds equally for both beams, the factor of 2 cancels in the ratio. Because the known laser serves as the ruler, the speed and distance of the mirror travel need not be known accurately. Precise measurements also correct for the wavelength dependence of the refractive index of air (of the order of 10⁻⁶).

measurement-027.question: In a phase-shifting interferometer, the reference mirror is moved to shift the interference phase by 0, π/2, π and 3π/2, giving intensities at one point of I₁ = 1.250, I₂ = 0.567, I₃ = 0.750 and I₄ = 1.433 (relative units). Finding the phase from tanφ = (I₄ − I₂)/(I₁ − I₃), in a reflection setup (the round trip makes the path difference twice the height) at a wavelength of 633 nm, which value is closest to the height of this point relative to a point of zero phase? (Assume no 2π ambiguity.)
choices: About 53 nm
About 105 nm
About 26 nm
measurement-027.explanation: tanφ = (1.433 − 0.567)/(1.250 − 0.750) = 0.866/0.500 ≈ 1.73, so φ ≈ 60°. In reflection a step of height h gives a round-trip path difference of 2h and a phase of 4πh/λ, so h = φλ/(4π) = (60°/360°) × 633 nm / 2 ≈ 53 nm. About 105 nm forgets the factor of 2 for the round trip and takes the path difference as h, and about 26 nm applies the factor of 2 twice. Because differences and ratios of the four images are used, uneven illumination and differences in reflectance (the mean and amplitude of the intensity) cancel, and surface shape can be measured to about a hundredth of a wavelength or better, far finer than reading fringe positions by eye.

measurement-028.question: A Shack–Hartmann wavefront sensor consists of a lenslet array (small lenses arranged in a grid) and an image sensor. Which correctly describes how it determines the shape of a wavefront?
choices: The intensity distribution behind each lenslet is taken directly as the wavefront height, with brighter spots treated as more advanced parts of the wavefront, to build the whole shape
The displacement of each lenslet's spot from its reference is proportional to the local wavefront slope, and the slopes are stitched together to obtain the shape
The fringes formed with a reference beam are counted within each lenslet, and each fringe is treated as one wavelength of wavefront delay to build up the whole shape
measurement-028.explanation: Each lenslet focuses part of the incoming wavefront onto its focal plane; if the wavefront is tilted there, the spot shifts sideways by the focal length times the tilt. The spot shifts of all lenslets give the distribution of local wavefront slopes, which is integrated to reconstruct the wavefront. Because no interference with a reference beam is used, the sensor works with white light and in vibrating environments, and it is used in adaptive optics for telescopes and for measuring aberrations of laser beams and of the eye. Counting fringes is how an interferometer works. Spot brightness reflects the intensity distribution and is not directly related to wavefront height.

measurement-029.question: Which correctly describes how the beam quality factor M² of a laser beam is measured?
choices: Focus the beam with a lens, measure the beam width at several points including near the waist and more than two Rayleigh lengths away, and fit the variation to a hyperbola
Measure the beam width precisely at a single far-field position well away from the waist and simply take that width divided by the wavelength as the beam's M², with no other positions needed
Measure the intensity profile at the waist and take the size of its deviation from a Gaussian shape directly as the beam's M²
measurement-029.explanation: The beam radius varies along the propagation as a hyperbola, w(z)² = w₀²[1 + ((z − z₀)/zR)²] with zR = πw₀²/(M²λ). M² compares the product of the waist radius and the far-field divergence, w₀θ, with λ/π for an ideal Gaussian beam of the same wavelength, so both the waist size and the spreading are needed. The beam is therefore focused with a lens to create a waist, and widths defined by second moments or similar are measured at several points, including near the waist and more than two Rayleigh lengths away, then fitted. A width at a single position cannot separate the waist size from the divergence. A profile close to Gaussian can still have a large M² if its phase is distorted, so the shape alone does not determine it either.

measurement-030.question: Heterodyne laser interferometers for precision positioning use two polarization components with slightly different frequencies. Which is a correct advantage over a homodyne interferometer that uses a single frequency?
choices: The two frequencies do not interfere, so the arm-length difference may exceed the coherence length and the laser linewidth does not matter
The frequency difference gives the absolute distance at once, so the mirror position is known immediately after power-up without returning to a home position
Mirror motion is measured as phase changes of a beat signal at a few MHz, so it resists intensity fluctuations and DC drift and can tell the direction of motion
measurement-030.explanation: In a heterodyne interferometer, two components at frequencies f₁ and f₂ (a few MHz apart) are sent to the measurement and reference arms and then recombined, and the beat signal at the difference frequency is detected. When the mirror moves at velocity v, the Doppler effect raises or lowers the beat frequency by 2v/λ, so counting its phase against a reference signal gives both the displacement and its direction. Because the signal is AC, it is little affected by changes in optical intensity or DC drift in the detector. What is measured, however, is a relative displacement accumulated from phase changes, so the origin must be reset after power-up. The two components are made to interfere on the detector to produce the beat, so they do interfere, and the arm-length difference must stay within the coherence length.

measurement-031.question: The polarization purity of a linearly polarized laser beam is measured as the ratio of minimum to maximum transmitted power (the extinction ratio) while an analyzer (assumed ideal) is rotated. Even if the light is perfectly linearly polarized, what is the ratio of the transmitted power to its maximum, in dB, when the analyzer is read at a position 1.0° away from the angle of minimum transmission? Which value is closest? (Assume transmission follows Malus's law, I = I₀cos²θ.)
choices: About −35 dB
About −18 dB
About −70 dB
measurement-031.explanation: The angle of minimum transmission lies 90° from the maximum, so a 1.0° offset gives θ = 91° and a transmission ratio of cos²91° = sin²1.0° ≈ (0.01745)² ≈ 3.0×10⁻⁴. In decibels this is 10 log₁₀(3.0×10⁻⁴) ≈ −35 dB, so even perfectly linear light would be measured with an extinction ratio of only about 35 dB. About −18 dB drops the square and takes sin1.0° itself as the ratio. About −70 dB wrongly applies 20 log₁₀ to a power ratio; power ratios are expressed with 10 log₁₀. Near the minimum the transmission grows with the square of the angular offset, so measuring 40 dB or more requires setting the minimum to better than 0.5°, and the extinction ratio of the analyzer itself also limits what can be measured.

measurement-032.question: In a Michelson interferometer using a He-Ne laser with a vacuum wavelength of 632.8 nm, the displacement of the movable mirror is obtained by multiplying the number of counted fringes by half the vacuum wavelength. If no correction is made for the refractive index of air, 1.00028, which value is closest to the error for a displacement of 1 m?
choices: About 0.28 µm
About 2.8 mm
About 0.28 mm
measurement-032.explanation: The wavelength in air is λ₀/n, so a displacement L produces N = 2nL/λ₀ fringes. Multiplying by λ₀/2 gives nL, which exceeds the true displacement by (n − 1)L = 2.8×10⁻⁴ × 1 m ≈ 0.28 mm. A relative error of 2.8×10⁻⁴ is far larger than the interferometer's resolution (of order nm), so precision length measurements correct for the refractive index of air calculated from temperature, pressure and humidity. About 0.28 µm confuses mm with µm, and about 2.8 mm reads n − 1 as 2.8×10⁻³, an order of magnitude too large. The index of air changes by about 10⁻⁶ per 1 °C and about 3×10⁻⁷ per 1 hPa, so even after correction, errors in measuring the environment leave errors of order µm per metre.

measurement-033.question: The intensity profile of a laser beam is recorded with a camera, and the beam diameter is obtained by the D4σ method, which defines the diameter as four times the standard deviation σ of the intensity distribution (its second moment). Which statement about this method is correct?
choices: D4σ is the diameter of the circle containing exactly half the power, and for a Gaussian beam it equals the intensity full width at half maximum (FWHM)
For a Gaussian beam it equals the 1/e² intensity diameter, and since it is sensitive to background noise and light in the wings, background subtraction is essential
D4σ is computed only from the position and height of the peak, so it is unaffected by background noise or stray light at the image edges and needs no correction
measurement-033.explanation: If σ is the standard deviation obtained from the second moment of the intensity distribution, a Gaussian beam exp(−2x²/w²) has σ = w/2, so D4σ = 4σ = 2w, equal to the 1/e² diameter. The method can be applied to beams of any shape and is used in the standards for M² measurement. Because the second moment weights pixels more heavily the farther they are from the center, background noise or stray light in the wings inflates the diameter, so the background is subtracted and the calculation region is restricted first. The FWHM is about 0.59 times the 1/e² diameter and does not equal D4σ. The diameter of the circle containing half the power is also a different quantity. The position and height of the peak alone do not determine the spread of the distribution.

measurement-034.question: An OTDR measures a fiber that has a strongly reflecting connector joint 2 km from the launch end. A small reflection peak with no accompanying loss step also appears farther along, at 4 km. Which explanation of this peak is correct?
choices: It is a ghost from multiple reflection, light from the strong reflection making one more round trip to the launch connector, and not a real event
It is a sign of a fiber break at 4 km, and there is no loss step because the break has only partly opened
It is a reflection of backscattered light from stimulated Brillouin scattering, growing at the same position as the pulse power is raised
measurement-034.explanation: An OTDR derives distance from round-trip time. Light returned by the strong reflection at 2 km can be reflected again by the launch connector and once more at the 2 km point before returning, travelling 8 km in total and arriving at the same time as an event at 4 km. A peak without a loss step (a ghost) therefore appears at exactly twice the distance of a strong reflection. It can be distinguished from a real event because the backscatter level is the same before and after it, and it can be reduced with low-reflection APC connectors or index-matching gel. A break would cut off or sharply lower the backscatter there, so it would not appear as a peak without a step. Stimulated Brillouin scattering generates frequency-shifted light along the whole fiber and does not create a peak at a fixed position.

measurement-035.question: You want to observe the longitudinal modes of a He-Ne laser, spaced by 150 MHz within a gain width of about 1.5 GHz, with a Fabry–Perot interferometer whose mirror spacing is scanned. Which interferometer is the most suitable? (Take the resolution as FSR/finesse.)
choices: An interferometer with an FSR of 300 MHz and a finesse of 1000 (resolution 0.3 MHz)
An interferometer with an FSR of 100 GHz and a finesse of 100 (resolution 1 GHz)
An interferometer with an FSR of 2 GHz and a finesse of 200 (resolution 10 MHz)
measurement-035.explanation: In a scanning Fabry–Perot interferometer the transmission peaks repeat every FSR, so unless the FSR exceeds the full width of the spectrum being measured, peaks from adjacent orders overlap and the mode pattern cannot be read. To separate the modes, the resolution FSR/finesse must also be much finer than the 150 MHz mode spacing. The interferometer with an FSR of 2 GHz and a finesse of 200 fits the whole 1.5 GHz within one FSR and separates the modes with a resolution of 10 MHz. The 300 MHz FSR instrument has high resolution, but the 1.5 GHz spectrum folds over five orders. The instrument with an FSR of 100 GHz and a finesse of 100 has a resolution of 1 GHz and cannot separate modes 150 MHz apart.
